summary: Shows how GMPLS control protocols can be extended to control SDH and SONET optical transport networks. It highlights routing extensions for distributing information used in path computation, and signaling extensions for setting up circuits. It also discusses new capabilities such as restoration methods and multi-layer circuit setup. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Old telephone fibre networks were set up by hand. This memo shows how to use the newer smart control system so they can plan routes and fix themselves.

questions: how does gmpls control sdh/sonet networks
how does gmpls routing work for optical networks
what are the benefits of gmpls for circuit switching
subtitle: Framework for applying IP control protocols to optical transport networks.

tldr.problem: Traditional SDH/SONET optical networks require manual, centralized management to provision circuits, which is slow and error-prone.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4257 describes how to extend GMPLS (Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching) to provide automated, distributed control of SDH/SONET networks using routing and signaling protocols similar to those used for IP networks.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can establish circuits dynamically, automatically find paths through the network, enable multi-layer switching and restoration, and reduce provisioning time from weeks to seconds.

today: RFC 4257 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It remains the framework reference for GMPLS control of SDH/SONET networks. Actual protocol specifications for GMPLS signaling and routing are defined in other RFCs like RFC 3471 and RFC 3472.

sections.title: Why Control SDH/SONET with GMPLS?
sections.content:
SDH (Synchronous Digital Hierarchy) and SONET (Synchronous Optical Networking) are the dominant standards for optical transport networks. They provide reliable, high-capacity circuits but have traditionally required manual provisioning by operators.

GMPLS is a suite of protocols extending MPLS to control networks beyond IP packets, including optical and circuit-switched systems. RFC 4257 shows how GMPLS can bring dynamic, distributed control to SDH/SONET networks. Instead of operators manually ordering circuits via forms and waiting weeks, customers and provisioning systems could request circuits in real-time, with the network automatically computing paths, avoiding congestion, and configuring the necessary equipment.
sections.eli5: Old fibre networks need human operators to set up each phone call route by hand. GMPLS is like giving the network a brain that can do this automatically.

sections.title: SDH/SONET Multiplexing and Switching
sections.content:
SDH and SONET networks are built on time-division multiplexing. A basic SDH signal (STM-1) operates at about 155 Mbps and consists of frames of transport overhead and payload. The payload contains a Virtual Container (VC) in SDH or Payload Envelope (SPE) in SONET. These can be multiplexed and concatenated to create higher-speed signals.

The SDH/SONET hierarchy has a tree structure. For example, an STM-1 can contain one VC-4, which can be subdivided into VC-3s and VC-2s, which can be further subdivided into VC-12s and VC-11s. SONET has a similar hierarchy with STS and VT signals. When GMPLS controls these networks, it treats each switchable element of this hierarchy as a potential Label Switched Path (LSP). The key constraint is that only elements referenced by pointers can be switched between inputs and outputs.
sections.eli5: A fibre can carry a huge signal that contains smaller signals nested like Russian dolls. Telephone calls go into the smallest level, and each level can be switched separately.

sections.title: GMPLS Routing: Sharing Network Information
sections.content:
For GMPLS to work on SDH/SONET networks, routers need to know what circuits are available. Traditional SDH/SONET networks did not share this information automatically; operators maintained it manually via management systems.

RFC 4257 shows that GMPLS uses link-state routing protocols (similar to IS-IS and OSPF used for IP) to advertise network topology and resource availability. The routing extensions must convey three key capabilities: switching granularity (which SDH/SONET hierarchy levels each node can switch), concatenation support (whether nodes can combine multiple signals), and transparency (whether nodes preserve overhead bits when switching higher-order signals). The routing protocol must also advertise protection properties (whether a link is ring-protected or linear 1+1 protected) so the path computation algorithm can make service-appropriate routing choices.
sections.eli5: Routers need to broadcast: what levels can I switch, can I glue signals together, do I have protection, and how much space is free? Link-state routing does that.

sections.title: GMPLS Signaling: Setting Up Circuits
sections.content:
Once a path is computed, GMPLS uses signaling protocols to configure the network equipment. In SDH/SONET, a label is not a header or VCI field; instead, it is a reference to a position in the multiplexing structure, such as a specific VC-12 slot or time-slot number. This label is local to each link—adjacent switches need to agree on which multiplex entry to use, but the numbering is different on each link.

The signaling protocol carries several pieces of information along the path: the label (the multiplex position), the bandwidth and priority of the circuit, the preemption characteristics (whether the circuit can be bumped for higher-priority traffic), and the payload type (what tributary signal is being transported). Each switch configures its input port, internal cross-connect fabric, and output port according to the signaling message, creating the end-to-end circuit.
sections.eli5: Signaling says: "Use slot 5 on this fibre, slot 12 on the next one, priority high, can't be bumped." Each switch writes that down and sets up its wires.

sections.title: New Capabilities and Deployment Models
sections.content:
Applying GMPLS to SDH/SONET networks enables capabilities that traditional management cannot provide. Multi-layer circuits become possible: a path can traverse multiple layers (IP, SDH/SONET, and optical wavelength) with a single signaling request. Restoration and recovery become faster and more flexible because the network can compute alternate paths in seconds without human intervention. Preemption allows high-priority services to bump lower-priority circuits, and ring-based protection strategies can be automatically coordinated.

Two deployment models are possible: centralized, where a management system calculates paths and triggers signaling, and distributed, where switches share topology information and each computes paths locally. The RFC notes that both are valid; the choice depends on network size, vendor capabilities, and operator preference. Centralized systems are easier to upgrade with new optimization features, while distributed systems provide faster restoration and better scalability.
sections.eli5: With GMPLS, the network can fix itself in seconds, route calls through multiple layers, and let important services bump unimportant ones. Operators can add new features by updating one management system.
